title: Cyber Incidents Doubled Since May. Cyber Premiums Rose 7%
summary: Marsh clients reported 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October, up 119% from 48 in late May, and Marsh links much of the rise to AI. Global cyber premiums are growing far more slowly, 6.9% this year. We set the two side by side and explain what it means for buyers at renewal.
description:
Cyber incidents are rising much faster than cyber insurance prices. Data from broker Marsh, reported by Reuters this week, shows its clients reported 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October 2026, more than double the 48 recorded in the final two weeks of May. Meredith Schnur, who leads Marsh Risk's US and Canada cyber practice, said a significant number could be attributed to artificial intelligence, as attackers use AI tools to find weaknesses faster and organisations take longer to contain attacks.

This PolicyRix Team analysis compares the incident trend with the premium trend and sets out what buyers should expect.

The numbers side by side

On our arithmetic, 105 incidents against 48 is a rise of about 119%, or about 2.2 times. Per day, that is about 7.5 incidents against about 3.4.

Premiums are moving much more gently. Marsh expects global cyber insurance premiums to grow 6.9% in 2026 to $16.6 billion, which implies about $15.5 billion in 2025, before growth accelerates to 10% in 2027, reaching $18.3 billion. Over the two years from 2025 to 2027, that is about 18% growth in total premiums.

Comparing an incident count with premium growth is not like for like, but the gap is striking: incidents reported by one broker's clients more than doubled within five months, while the market's total premium is expected to grow by less than a fifth over two years.

Why prices have not caught up

The cyber market spent 2024 and 2025 in a soft phase. After heavy price rises in 2021 and 2022, new capacity arrived and premiums fell or flattened as insurers competed. Marsh's UK outlook earlier this year described rising demand and expanded capacity keeping premiums relatively low. Insurance prices react to claims after a lag, typically once insurers see a year of losses develop. A two-week spike in notifications will not move prices on its own, but a sustained rise will.

This month has added to the pressure. The Microsoft 365 outage on November 12 tested business interruption cover, and the $6.3 billion Binance theft showed how social engineering can defeat technical controls. Both reinforce the case for tighter underwriting even before the incident data is fully reflected in loss ratios.

What it means for buyers

Expect renewals in 2027 to look different from 2025 and 2026. On Marsh's forecast, the market grows 10% next year, which would come partly from new buyers and partly from higher rates. Underwriters will also ask harder questions about AI: how staff use AI tools, whether AI agents can move money or data, and how quickly an incident can be contained. Some insurers are adding AI exclusions to general liability policies, and new standalone AI products are appearing.

Practical steps before renewal: document controls such as multi-factor authentication, offline backups and an incident response plan, since these drive price and terms. Check whether the policy covers social engineering losses and at what sub-limit. Check whether it responds to AI-driven incidents and to outages at technology providers. And consider locking in terms early if your renewal is in the first half of 2027.

What the data cannot tell us

The incident figures cover Marsh clients only and two short windows, which can be noisy. They count reported incidents, not claims, and many incidents never become claims. Attribution to AI is an expert judgement rather than a measured share. The premium figures are forecasts. And premium growth combines more buyers with higher prices, so it does not show the price change for an individual company.

The short version: attacks are accelerating faster than prices, which usually means cyber insurance is about to get tighter, and buyers who prepare now will get better terms.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of Marsh data reported by Reuters (via The Star and Claims Journal), Marsh 2026 cyber outlook
image_alt: Computer screen with code and security graphics (illustrative)
key_points: Marsh clients reported 105 cyber incidents in late October, up 119% from 48 in late May.
Marsh's Meredith Schnur attributes a significant share of the rise to AI tools used by attackers.
Marsh expects cyber premiums to grow 6.9% to $16.6 billion in 2026 and 10% to $18.3 billion in 2027.
On our calculation, premiums grow about 18% over two years while incidents more than doubled in five months.
Buyers should document controls and check social engineering and AI cover before 2027 renewals.
why_it_matters: When incidents rise faster than premiums, insurers usually respond with higher prices and tighter terms. Businesses that see the shift coming can prepare and lock in better cover.

title: Impersonation Scams: Why Most Insurance Won't Pay You Back
summary: Nearly 60% of scam cases at Allstate Identity Protection this year involved impersonation, and more than 90% were paid by crypto, wire, gift card or payment apps. Most policies exclude money you send voluntarily. We compare US cover with the UK's bank reimbursement rules.
description:
The most common scam in America is now someone pretending to be someone you trust. Allstate Identity Protection said on October 29 that impersonation made up nearly 60% of the scam cases it handled from January to September 2026, and that more than 90% of its scam cases involved payment by cryptocurrency, wire transfer, gift cards or peer-to-peer payment apps. The Federal Trade Commission reported in June that Americans lost $3.5 billion to imposter scams in 2025, nearly three times the 2020 total, and that impersonation has been the most reported fraud category for five years running.

The problem for victims is that most insurance does not cover this kind of loss. This PolicyRix Team analysis explains why, and compares the US with the UK, where banks must reimburse most victims.

Why insurance usually says no

In an impersonation scam the victim sends the money. A caller posing as a bank, a relative, the police or a delivery firm persuades them to move funds. Because the victim authorised the payment, many crime and cyber policies apply what is called a voluntary parting exclusion: there is no cover when the policyholder chose to hand over money, even if they were deceived. US courts have upheld this exclusion in business cases where employees were tricked into wiring funds.

Social engineering cover, which does respond to deception, exists mostly for businesses and is often subject to low sub-limits and strict conditions, such as having verified the payment request by phone. Personal identity theft policies are designed for stolen identities, not for money someone was talked into sending. Homeowners policies rarely help, beyond limited cover for forged cheques or credit card misuse in some forms.

The payment methods make it worse. Crypto, wire transfers and gift cards are hard or impossible to reverse, and US rules on unauthorised transfers do not generally protect a payment the account holder authorised, even under false pretences.

A new kind of product

Some insurers are starting to fill the gap. Allstate's Scam Protection benefit, sold through employer benefits plans, reimburses up to $50,000 a year for covered scam losses, including some crypto scams, which Allstate describes as the first offer of its kind at that scale from a major US insurer. Allstate also offers free identity theft protection to about 7.5 million eligible customers in 44 states, though that is focused on identity restoration rather than reimbursing money sent to scammers.

How the UK does it differently

The UK took a different path. Since October 2024, payment firms have been required to reimburse most victims of authorised push payment fraud, the UK term for scams where victims send money themselves, up to a cap of GBP 85,000 per claim, with the cost split between the sending and receiving firms. Exceptions apply, such as gross negligence. The rule covers bank transfers made through the Faster Payments system, not crypto or gift cards.

Take an illustrative victim tricked into sending $20,000, or the equivalent, by bank transfer. In the UK, under that framework, they would generally get it back from their bank. In the US, they would usually depend on the bank's goodwill, a specialist scam benefit if they had one, or recovery through law enforcement, which is rare.

What you can do

Prevention matters far more than insurance. Hang up and call back on a number you find yourself. Treat any request to pay by crypto, gift card or wire as a red flag; real banks, government agencies and companies do not ask for these. Agree a family code word for emergency calls. Check whether your employer offers scam protection in its benefits. For businesses, check for social engineering cover and its sub-limit, and require call-back verification for any change to payment details. If you are scammed, contact your bank immediately, report to the FTC and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, and keep records.

What the data cannot tell us

Allstate's figures cover its own customers and may not represent all Americans. FTC losses include only reported cases, and most scams go unreported. Policy terms vary widely, so some readers may have more cover than this general picture suggests; read your own policy. The UK comparison describes the rules as introduced; individual outcomes depend on the facts of each case.

The short version: in the US, money you are tricked into sending is usually yours to lose, so the best protection is not to send it.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of Allstate Identity Protection data (Oct 29, 2026), FTC Consumer Sentinel figures, Insurance Business and Insurance Journal reporting, and UK Payment Systems Regulator rules
key_points: Nearly 60% of Allstate Identity Protection's 2026 scam cases involved impersonation.
More than 90% were paid by crypto, wire, gift cards or peer-to-peer apps, which are hard to reverse.
Americans lost $3.5 billion to imposter scams in 2025, nearly three times 2020, per the FTC.
Most crime and cyber policies exclude voluntary transfers, even when the victim was deceived.
The UK requires firms to reimburse most bank-transfer scam victims up to GBP 85,000; the US has no equivalent.
why_it_matters: Many people assume insurance or their bank will cover a scam. In the US that is usually not true, so knowing the gap is the first step to avoiding a permanent loss.

title: German Car Insurance: Prices Flatten Before the Nov 30 Switch Date
summary: New German car insurance policies cost only about 2% more than a year ago, after a 25% jump in 2024, and budget cover is about 2% cheaper. With 12.5 million drivers getting a new type class for 2027, we show what the numbers mean before the November 30 switching deadline.
description:
Every November, millions of German drivers compare car insurance before the usual cancellation date of November 30. This year, for the first time in three years, the comparison may actually save money. The Verivox insurance index, calculated with the Technical University of Augsburg, shows that new policies at the start of the switching season cost on average about 2% more than a year earlier, below the general inflation rate. In the budget segment, prices are on average almost 2% lower.

This PolicyRix Team analysis puts that figure in context and works through what it means for a typical driver.

Three years of steep increases

2024 was the record year, with new policies up by just under 25% on average. Verivox says car insurance now costs more than 50% more on average than in 2022. The main driver is repair costs: the German insurance association GDV says spare parts prices have risen about 80% since 2016, which on our calculation is about 6% a year compounded. At one point the motor line as a whole slipped into loss for insurers.

2025 and 2026 were better years for insurers, partly because Germany largely escaped severe storms and other natural catastrophes, and that is now showing up in prices.

This year's changes by type of cover

According to Verivox, for mid-range policies, third-party liability (Haftpflicht) is up 3.1%, partial cover (Teilkasko) up 0.4% and comprehensive cover (Vollkasko) up 1.6%. In the budget segment, liability is down 1.2%, partial cover down 1% and comprehensive down 2.3%. Verivox's Aljoscha Ziller cautions that this is not yet a lasting turn in prices. Existing contracts are also still becoming more expensive, which is the main reason to compare.

What it means in euros

Take an illustrative driver who paid EUR 600 for a new policy in 2022. A rise of 50% takes that to about EUR 900 today. A further 2% rise on the average new policy would mean about EUR 918; a 2% fall in the budget segment would mean about EUR 882. If the driver's existing insurer raises the renewal price by more than the market, switching could save a noticeable amount. These are our illustrations; actual prices depend on the car, location, driver and no-claims class.

Type and regional classes for 2027

Two official classifications also move each year. The GDV has recalculated the type classes (Typklassen) for 2027 across about 33,000 car models. For liability cover, about 7.4 million drivers move to a higher class and about 5.1 million to a lower one, while about 30 million, or 71%, stay the same. The regional classes, recalculated for all 413 registration districts, improve for about 5.2 million drivers in 63 districts and worsen for about 4.8 million in 46 districts. A higher class usually means a higher premium, but each insurer translates the classes into prices differently.

How to switch well

Check your renewal notice for the new price and any change in type or regional class. Compare at least the same level of cover, including the excess, workshop tie-ins (Werkstattbindung) and protection for your no-claims class. A policy with workshop tie-in is usually cheaper but restricts where repairs are done. If your insurer raises the premium without changing cover, you usually have a special right to cancel within a month of the notice, even after November 30. Check your own contract, since cancellation dates depend on its terms.

What the data cannot tell us

The Verivox index covers new policies sold through its comparison platform and model profiles, not all contracts. Averages hide wide differences between drivers. The type and regional class figures count drivers affected, not the size of any price change. And a good claims year can turn quickly: a single severe hailstorm season would push prices up again.

The short version: after three years of steep rises, German car insurance prices have levelled off, which makes this year's comparison before November 30 more worthwhile than usual.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of the Verivox insurance index (via dpa/autohaus.de, October 2026), GDV type and regional class statistics for 2027, and ADAC
key_points: New German car insurance policies cost about 2% more than a year ago; budget policies about 2% less, per Verivox.
Prices rose just under 25% in 2024 and are more than 50% above 2022.
Spare parts prices are up about 80% since 2016, roughly 6% a year on our calculation.
For 2027, 7.4 million drivers get a higher type class, 5.1 million a lower one; 71% are unchanged.
November 30 is the usual cancellation date; a price rise without changed cover usually gives a special right to cancel.
why_it_matters: Car insurance is one of the largest fixed costs for German drivers. With prices flattening after three years of sharp rises, this year's switching season offers a real chance to save.

title: Insurance Broker Deals Hit an Eight-Year Low as Buyers Narrow
summary: US and Canadian insurance agency deals fell 27% in the third quarter to 144, and the 600 deals in the past year are the fewest since 2018. Only 82 buyers were active, and the top tenth closed 55% of deals. We explain what consolidation means for policyholders.
description:
The buying spree that has reshaped insurance distribution in North America is slowing. Investment bank OPTIS Partners counted 144 insurance agency and broker acquisitions in the US and Canada in the third quarter of 2026, down 27% from 197 a year earlier, though up 3% from the second quarter. Over the first nine months there were 439 deals, down 19% from 539.

This PolicyRix Team analysis looks at what the numbers say about who is buying, and what consolidation means for the people and businesses who buy insurance through agents.

The slowdown in numbers

On a rolling 12-month basis, 600 deals were announced to the end of September, down 21% from 763 a year earlier. That is the lowest total since the second quarter of 2018, when 578 deals were logged. Year-to-date volume is about 30% below the previous five-year average.

Fewer buyers, bigger shares

The more telling change is who is buying. Only 82 unique buyers were active over the past four quarters. For the first time, private equity-backed buyers, 43 of them, outnumbered all other types of buyer combined, 39. Private equity-backed and hybrid buyers were involved in 76% of transactions. The top 10% of acquirers accounted for 55% of deals.

On our arithmetic, 600 deals among 82 buyers is about 7.3 deals per buyer. The most active, BroadStreet Partners, completed 69 deals over the past 12 months, about 11.5% of all deals by itself. Only eight firms closed 20 or more deals, the fewest since 2020.

Why buying has slowed

OPTIS says most private equity-backed platforms still want to buy, but are under pressure to reduce debt, integrate past acquisitions and prepare their own sale or recapitalisation. Higher interest rates make debt-funded deals more expensive. OPTIS partner Steve Germundson said deal flow has been slower than expected, though the firm expects some pick-up in the fourth quarter.

What it means for policyholders

Most people never notice when their local agency is bought. The agent, phone number and office often stay the same. But consolidation can change things over time. Larger groups may consolidate the insurers they place business with, which can mean fewer options for unusual risks. Service may move to central teams. Fees and commission arrangements can change. On the positive side, larger agencies often have access to more insurers and specialist programmes, and better technology.

What customers can do

If your agency has been acquired, ask whether your account manager and the insurers they use will change, and whether any fees apply. At renewal, ask how many insurers the agency approached for your cover. For businesses, check that the broker still has specialists in your industry. And remember you can move your account to another agent if service declines; in most cases it is a matter of signing a broker of record letter.

What the data cannot tell us

OPTIS counts announced deals; many small deals go unannounced, so the true number is higher. Deal counts say nothing about deal size or prices paid, and fewer deals can coexist with large amounts of capital. The figures cover the US and Canada only. And the data does not measure service quality before and after a sale.

The short version: fewer, larger buyers are now doing most of the deals, and the market is pausing rather than stopping, so consolidation of insurance distribution is likely to continue.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of OPTIS Partners Q3 2026 M&A data, via Insurance Journal, Insurance Business, Business Insurance and Risk & Insurance
key_points: US and Canadian agency deals fell 27% in Q3 2026 to 144; nine-month deals fell 19% to 439.
The 600 deals over 12 months are the fewest since Q2 2018.
Only 82 buyers were active; private equity-backed buyers (43) outnumbered all others (39) for the first time.
The top 10% of acquirers closed 55% of deals; BroadStreet alone did about 11.5% on our calculation.
Policyholders of acquired agencies should ask about changes to insurers, service teams and fees.
why_it_matters: Most insurance in North America is sold through agents and brokers. Who owns them shapes the choice of insurers, service and fees that customers get.

title: MAS Offers S$30m and Lower Capital Charges for Infrastructure
summary: Singapore's regulator will set aside S$30 million to help insurers build infrastructure investment teams and is consulting until December 18 on lower capital charges for qualifying infrastructure debt, equity and senior securitisation tranches.
description:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) wants insurers to put more of their long-term money into Asian infrastructure, and it is changing the rules to make that easier. Announced on November 2 by Chee Hong Tat, Minister for National Development and MAS deputy chairman, at the Singapore International Reinsurance Conference, the package combines a grant, proposed capital changes and simpler assessment processes.

What changed

First, MAS has set aside S$30 million under its Financial Sector Development Fund for an Infrastructure Capability Development Grant for Insurers, effective immediately. It can fund the cost of building dedicated infrastructure investment teams, training existing staff, and hiring professional services to start or expand infrastructure investing.

Second, MAS is consulting on changes to its risk-based capital framework for insurers. Rated infrastructure debt that meets specified credit quality and other requirements would attract lower capital charges. So would qualifying infrastructure equity and debt with risk-reducing features, such as revenues backed by long-term contracts, limited exposure to demand swings, and support from strong-credit counterparties. Senior, investment-grade securitisation tranches that meet criteria for simplicity, transparency and comparability, or conditions such as portfolio diversification and liquidity safeguards, would also get lower charges. The consultation closes on December 18, 2026.

Third, MAS will recognise more credit rating agencies with expertise in infrastructure and securitisation. Fourth, it is working with the industry on standard disclosure templates, clearer assessment guidance and fund-manager declarations to make due diligence more consistent.

Why it matters

Insurers are natural long-term investors because they hold money for years to pay future claims and pensions, especially in life insurance. Infrastructure, such as power, transport and data centres, offers long-dated, steady cash flows that can match those liabilities. Asia needs large amounts of infrastructure investment, and governments cannot fund all of it.

But capital rules decide how attractive an asset is. If an investment carries a high capital charge, the insurer must hold more capital against it, which lowers the return on that capital. By tying charges more closely to actual risk, MAS aims to stop rules from penalising safer infrastructure projects. Europe and the UK have made similar changes under Solvency II for qualifying infrastructure.

What it means for policyholders

For policyholders, the key question is whether insurers can earn better returns without taking risks that could threaten claims. MAS says it will keep prudential standards and policyholder protection in place, and the lower charges apply only to assets that meet the qualifying conditions. Over time, higher investment returns can support better bonuses on participating policies or more competitive pricing for annuities and savings products. The risk is that infrastructure investments are illiquid and harder to value; MAS's emphasis on expertise, ratings and standard disclosures is designed to address that.

This builds on earlier steps. MAS refined capital treatment for structured products and infrastructure investments in its Notice 133 earlier in 2026, and has proposed a protected cell company structure to grow captives and insurance-linked securities in Singapore.

What to watch

The consultation paper sets out the detailed capital charges and eligibility tests, and the final rules will determine how much difference the changes make. Insurers, fund managers and other interested parties can send comments to MAS until the December 18 deadline. Watch for how many insurers apply for the grant, whether large regional insurers move infrastructure teams to Singapore, and whether the measures lead to new infrastructure funds aimed at insurance investors.
source_name: Monetary Authority of Singapore media release and keynote speech (November 2, 2026)
key_points: MAS has set aside S$30 million for a grant to help insurers build infrastructure investment capabilities.
It proposes lower capital charges for qualifying infrastructure debt, equity and senior securitisation tranches.
The consultation closes on December 18, 2026.
MAS will recognise more rating agencies with infrastructure and securitisation expertise.
Standard disclosure templates and assessment guidance aim to simplify due diligence.
why_it_matters: How insurers invest premiums affects their safety and the returns behind life and savings products. Singapore is trying to channel more of that money into infrastructure without weakening protection.

title: UAE Insurers: Profits Up 46%, but Seven Miss Solvency Rules
summary: AM Best says listed UAE insurers lifted net profit 46% in 2025 on 17% revenue growth, pushing return on equity to 11.7%. But seven listed insurers, about 12% of market revenue, breach solvency rules, and medical inflation of about 11.5% threatens health margins.
description:
The UAE insurance market had an exceptional 2025, but AM Best's latest review shows the gains are uneven. According to the rating agency, insurance revenue for listed UAE insurers rose 17% in 2025, driven by rate increases, portfolio growth and better pricing discipline, while consolidated net profit after tax rose 46%. Average return on equity rose to 11.7% from 8.9%.

This PolicyRix Team analysis looks behind the headline numbers at what drove them, and at the risks AM Best flags.

Margins, not just growth

When profit grows faster than revenue, margins are widening. On our arithmetic, profit growing 46% while revenue grew 17% means the profit margin on each dirham of revenue rose by about a quarter. Return on equity rising 2.8 percentage points, from 8.9% to 11.7%, is a relative improvement of about 31%.

Two things helped. There were no major catastrophe losses in 2025, after the severe April 2024 rainfall that flooded parts of Dubai and caused heavy motor and property claims. And motor pricing improved sharply: AM Best says rate increases and better customer segmentation lifted average motor revenues by about 30%, though rising repair costs still pressure parts of the book.

The pressure points

Health insurance is the biggest risk to margins. AM Best estimates UAE medical inflation at about 11.5%. On our calculation, costs rising at that rate would double in a little over six years. With health cover now mandatory across all emirates, AM Best expects loss ratios to worsen as policyholders use their cover more.

Solvency is the other concern. Seven listed insurers are in breach of regulatory solvency requirements, AM Best says, together representing about 12% of market revenue. The UAE Central Bank, which supervises insurers, is increasing its focus on solvency and climate risk. Consolidation is a likely outcome for weaker players, as has happened elsewhere in the Gulf.

Investments add volatility. Insurers hold significant real estate and equity investments, which market swings have affected, though AM Best considers balance sheets resilient overall.

War cover and the regional conflict

Standard UAE insurance policies typically exclude war risks. Such cover is sold separately and largely passed to international reinsurers. War-related losses for domestic insurers have been minimal so far because of heavy use of facultative reinsurance and low retention. But AM Best warns that any rise in reinsurance costs from continued regional instability would be passed on to policyholders. Some insurers have grown sharply by writing marine war cover, which is fully reinsured.

Reinsurance strategy has also shifted. After the 2024 floods and rising reinsurance prices, many UAE insurers have moved from quota share arrangements, where reinsurers take a fixed share of every policy, toward excess of loss cover, which pays only above a set loss level. That keeps more premium, and more risk, with the insurer.

What it means for policyholders

For motor customers, the 30% rise in average motor revenue reflects higher premiums, which are unlikely to fall soon. Health insurance renewals are likely to keep rising with medical inflation. Businesses buying property cover should check war and terrorism exclusions and ask about separate cover where relevant. And customers of smaller insurers can check AM Best or other ratings and the insurer's published solvency figures; regulators protect policyholders if an insurer fails, but switching from a weak insurer at renewal is simpler.

What the data cannot tell us

The figures cover listed insurers only, not the whole market, and AM Best did not publish combined ratios. A benign catastrophe year flatters results, so 2025 may not be repeatable. The solvency breaches are counted by number of insurers and revenue share, not by the size of the capital shortfall.

The short version: UAE insurers are more profitable than ever on average, but rising medical costs, solvency gaps at smaller firms and regional risk mean the strong year may not last.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of AM Best's UAE market segment report, via Global Reinsurance and Business Wire
key_points: Listed UAE insurers grew revenue 17% and net profit 46% in 2025; ROE rose to 11.7% from 8.9%.
On our calculation, profit margins rose by about a quarter.
Motor revenues rose about 30% on rate increases and better segmentation.
Medical inflation of about 11.5% would double costs in a little over six years.
Seven listed insurers, about 12% of market revenue, breach solvency requirements.
why_it_matters: Insurer profits and solvency decide how reliably claims get paid and how premiums move. The UAE's record year hides pressure from health costs and weaker insurers.
